# Using PLINK from R and RStudio {#sec-rstudio}

::: {.lead}
PLINK does the heavy lifting; R draws the pictures. Running both from one RStudio project means your commands, results and plots live in one place, and you can re-run the whole analysis with one click.
:::

There is no "PLINK package" that replaces the PLINK program. In R we do one of two things: we **call the PLINK program** from R, or we **read PLINK's files** into R. This chapter shows both.

## Step 1: install R, RStudio and a few packages

1. Install R from <https://cran.r-project.org>.
2. Install RStudio Desktop from <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>.
3. In RStudio, install the packages used in this book:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "data.table", "bigsnpr", "genio", "plinkQC"))
```

## Step 2: make an RStudio project

Use **File > New Project > New Directory**, call it `plink_tutorial`, and put the PLINK program and the practice data in that folder. A project sets the working directory for you, so you never need `setwd()` with a long path that only works on your own computer.

```text
plink_tutorial/
  plink_tutorial.Rproj
  plink            (or plink.exe on Windows)
  data/            (cattle.ped, cattle.map, pheno.txt, ...)
  results/
  analysis.R       (or analysis.qmd)
```

## Step 3: get PLINK into the project

You have three choices. Use whichever works on your computer.

**Option A: download it by hand** (Chapter 1) and copy the file into the project folder.

**Option B: let R download it.** The `bigsnpr` package has helper functions that download the right PLINK build for your system and return its path:

```r
library(bigsnpr)
plink  <- download_plink(dir = ".")     # PLINK 1.9
plink2 <- download_plink2(dir = ".")    # PLINK 2.0
plink                                    # prints the full path, e.g. "./plink"
```

**Option C: use the RStudio Terminal.** RStudio has a **Terminal** tab next to the Console. It is a normal command line that opens in your project folder, so every command in this book works there unchanged.

## Step 4: run PLINK from R

R's `system2()` function runs an outside program. Give it the program path and the arguments:

```r
plink <- "./plink"           # on Windows: "plink.exe"

system2(plink, args = c("--file", "data/cattle", "--cow",
                        "--make-bed", "--out", "results/cattle"))
```

The older `system()` function takes the whole command as one string, which is handy for copying commands from this book:

```r
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --missing --out results/miss")
```

### A complete script with `system()`

Many people keep their whole analysis in one R script built around `system()`. Here is a typical one, written for the files of this book:

```r
# clear the workspace (removes your R objects; loaded packages stay loaded)
rm(list = ls())

# set the working directory: the folder that holds PLINK and the data
setwd("D:/genomics/plink_tutorial")        # Windows
# setwd("~/genomics/plink_tutorial")       # macOS or Linux

# run PLINK: read the binary files, convert them back to text
system("plink --bfile cattle --cow --nonfounders --allow-no-sex --recode --out cattle_QC_out")
```

What each part of the PLINK command does, and what it printed when we ran it:

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `plink` | The program. This works only if PLINK is on your PATH (Chapter 1). Otherwise give the path: `"./plink ..."` on macOS and Linux, `"plink.exe ..."` or `"D:/genomics/plink.exe ..."` on Windows |
| `--bfile cattle` | Read `cattle.bed`, `cattle.bim` and `cattle.fam` from the working directory |
| `--cow` | 29 cattle autosomes plus X, Y and MT |
| `--nonfounders` | Count all 361 animals, not only the 301 founders, when PLINK computes allele frequencies |
| `--allow-no-sex` | Keep the phenotypes of the two animals with unknown sex |
| `--recode` | Write text files: `cattle_QC_out.ped` and `.map` |
| `--out cattle_QC_out` | Start of every output file name |

```text
4800 variants loaded from .bim file.
361 cattle (137 males, 222 females, 2 ambiguous) loaded from .fam.
Before main variant filters, 301 founders and 60 nonfounders present.
Calculating allele frequencies... done.
Total genotyping rate is 0.992812.
4800 variants and 361 cattle pass filters and QC.
--recode ped to cattle_QC_out.ped + cattle_QC_out.map ... done.
```

It worked, but two things are worth knowing. First, this command does no QC at all: `--recode` only converts, and nothing was removed (4,800 SNPs and 361 animals in, the same out). Give the output a name that says what it is, such as `cattle_text`. Second, `--nonfounders` changes nothing you can see here. It only matters where PLINK computes allele frequencies: in `--freq`, `--hardy`, `--maf` and `--hwe`, and when it decides which allele is the minor one (A1). For example, `--freq` gave snp00001 a MAF of 0.0249 from the 301 founders (602 chromosomes) and 0.0292 with `--nonfounders` (720 chromosomes). Add a flag only when you know which step it changes.

Two R details. `system()` returns PLINK's exit status: 0 means success, anything else means PLINK stopped with an error, so `status <- system("plink ...")` followed by `if (status != 0) stop("PLINK failed")` stops a long script at the first problem. And `setwd()` with a full path ties the script to one computer; an RStudio project (Step 2) avoids that. (The PLINK output above is real; R itself was not available where this book was built, so the R lines are shown, not run.)

On Windows, write paths with forward slashes (`"C:/genomics/plink.exe"`) or doubled backslashes (`"C:\\genomics\\plink.exe"`). A single backslash breaks the string.

A small helper function saves typing and prints PLINK's messages in the Console:

```r
run_plink <- function(..., exe = "./plink") {
  args <- c(...)
  out <- system2(exe, args = args, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)
  cat(out, sep = "\n")
  invisible(out)
}

run_plink("--bfile", "results/cattle", "--cow", "--freq", "--out", "results/freq")
```

## Step 5: read the results into R

Almost every PLINK output is a plain text table with a header line and columns separated by spaces. `read.table(header = TRUE)` reads it, and `data.table::fread()` does the same faster for big files.

```r
library(tidyverse)

imiss <- read.table("results/miss.imiss", header = TRUE)
lmiss <- read.table("results/miss.lmiss", header = TRUE)

ggplot(imiss, aes(x = F_MISS * 100)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#E69F00") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Missing genotypes per animal (%)", y = "Number of animals",
       title = "Missingness per animal") +
  theme_minimal()
```

| PLINK output | How to read it in R |
|---|---|
| `.frq`, `.hwe`, `.imiss`, `.lmiss`, `.het`, `.genome`, `.assoc`, `.qassoc`, `.assoc.linear` | `read.table(file, header = TRUE)` |
| `.eigenvec` written with `--pca header` | `read.table(file, header = TRUE)` |
| `.eigenvec` written without `header` | `read.table(file, col.names = c("FID", "IID", paste0("PC", 1:20)))` |
| `.eigenval` | `scan(file)` (just a column of numbers) |
| `.mdist`, `.mibs`, `.rel` (square matrices) | `as.matrix(read.table(file))` |
| `.raw` from `--recode A` | `read.table(file, header = TRUE)`; genotypes start in column 7 |
| `.bed/.bim/.fam` themselves | `genio::read_plink("results/cattle")` or `bigsnpr::snp_readBed()` |

Reading the binary genotypes directly is useful when you want to fit your own models, for example genomic prediction:

```r
library(genio)
geno <- read_plink("results/cattle")
dim(geno$X)        # SNPs in rows, animals in columns, values 0/1/2 or NA
head(geno$bim)     # the SNP map; genio calls A1 "alt" and A2 "ref"
head(geno$fam)     # the animals
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Which allele is being counted?
Different tools count different alleles. `genio::read_plink()` counts copies of **A2** (the allele genio calls `ref`), while PLINK's own `--recode A` file and `bigsnpr` count copies of **A1**. For an animal that is A1/A1, genio gives 0 and `--recode A` gives 2. Before you combine genotypes from two tools, check one SNP by hand.
:::

## Step 6: let a package do routine QC for you

The `plinkQC` package by Hannah Meyer wraps PLINK's QC commands (missingness, heterozygosity, sex check, relatedness) and makes clear plots. It follows the QC protocol of Anderson and colleagues (2010).

```r
library(plinkQC)
# 1. run PLINK yourself, with the species flag
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --missing --out results/cattle")
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --het --out results/cattle")
# 2. let plinkQC read results/cattle.imiss and results/cattle.het and draw the plot
fail_miss_het <- check_het_and_miss(indir = "results", name = "cattle",
                                     run.check_het_and_miss = FALSE,
                                     imissTh = 0.03, hetTh = 3, interactive = TRUE)
```

plinkQC was written for human data, and the PLINK commands it runs for you carry no species flag, so on cattle files PLINK would stop at chromosome codes above 26. That is why the example runs PLINK itself with `--cow` and lets plinkQC only read and plot the results. Every check has a switch for this (`run.check_het_and_miss = FALSE` above, `run.check_sex = FALSE` in `check_sex()`), and it then looks for `<name>.imiss`, `<name>.het` or `<name>.sexcheck` in the folder you give.

## Keep a record

Write your commands in an R script or a Quarto notebook rather than typing them into the Console. Six months later, when a reviewer asks "which `--geno` threshold did you use?", the answer is in the file, together with the plot it produced.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
If `system2()` returns status 127 or "cannot find", R is not looking where PLINK is. Check with `file.exists(plink)`, and on macOS or Linux make the file executable once with `Sys.chmod(plink, mode = "0755")`.
:::

## Exercises

Try each question first, then open the answer. The challenge goes a step further than the chapter.

**1.** Use `system2()` to run `--freq` on `cattle`, then read `plink.frq` (or the file named by your `--out`) into R. How many SNPs have a MAF below 0.05?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```r
system2("./plink", c("--bfile", "cattle", "--cow", "--freq", "--out", "frq_all"))
frq <- read.table("frq_all.frq", header = TRUE)
sum(frq$MAF < 0.05)    # 802
sum(frq$MAF == 0)      # 83 monomorphic SNPs
```
:::

**Challenge.** Write a loop in R that runs `--freq` separately for each breed (using a keep file per breed) and prints the number of SNPs with MAF below 0.05 in each breed. Which breed has the most rare or fixed SNPs, and why might that be?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```r
fam <- read.table("cattle.fam")
for (b in c("ANG", "HOL", "NDA")) {
  write.table(fam[fam$V1 == b, 1:2], paste0("k_", b, ".txt"),
              quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)
  system2("./plink", c("--bfile", "cattle", "--cow", "--keep", paste0("k_", b, ".txt"),
                       "--freq", "--out", paste0("fr_", b)))
  f <- read.table(paste0("fr_", b, ".frq"), header = TRUE)
  cat(b, sum(f$MAF < 0.05), "SNPs with MAF < 0.05,", sum(f$MAF == 0), "fixed\n")
}
```
PLINK gave ANG 1,022 (375 fixed), HOL 1,009 (335 fixed) and NDA 1,358 (578 fixed). N'Dama has the most because, in this simulation, it is the breed that drifted furthest from the common ancestor (it has the highest F_ST), so more alleles were lost or fixed. In real data, ascertainment bias adds to this: chip SNPs are mostly chosen in European breeds, so fewer of them vary in African cattle (Chapter 18). Note that a SNP fixed in one breed can still be informative across breeds.
:::
